proofs.proof_tex:
Because \(X_0=\operatorname{supp}_P(X)\) is closed and \(X\in I\) almost surely with \(I\) compact, \(X_0\) is compact.  Every \(u\in\mathcal C_P\) satisfies
\[
\|u\|_\infty\le M,
\qquad
|u(x)-u(x')|\le L|x-x'|
\quad(x,x'\in X_0).
\]
Thus \(\mathcal C_P\) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous.  It is also closed in the uniform norm: if \(u_j\in\mathcal C_P\) and \(\|u_j-u\|_\infty\to0\), then for every \(x,x'\in X_0\) and \((x,z)\in H\), passage to the limit in the defining inequalities gives
\[
|u(x)|\le M,
\qquad
|u(x)-u(x')|\le L|x-x'|,
\qquad
|g(x,z)-u(x)|\le K|z|.
\]
Hence \(u\in\mathcal C_P\).  Compactness can be proved directly.  Let \((u_j)_{j\ge1}\) be any sequence in \(\mathcal C_P\), and choose a countable dense subset \(D\) of the compact subset \(X_0\subset\mathbb R\).  Since \(|u_j(x)|\le M\), successive subsequence extraction and a diagonal argument produce a subsequence \((u_{j_k})_k\) that converges at every point of \(D\).  Fix \(\epsilon>0\).  If \(L>0\), choose a finite \(\epsilon/(6L)\)-net \(D_\epsilon\subset D\) for \(X_0\); if \(L=0\), take any singleton in the nonempty set \(D\).  For all sufficiently large \(k,k'\), convergence on the finite set \(D_\epsilon\) gives
\[
\max_{d\in D_\epsilon}|u_{j_k}(d)-u_{j_{k'}}(d)|<\epsilon/3.
\]
For any \(x\in X_0\), choose \(d\in D_\epsilon\) within \(\epsilon/(6L)\) when \(L>0\).  The common Lipschitz bound then gives
\[
|u_{j_k}(x)-u_{j_{k'}}(x)|
\le L|x-d|+|u_{j_k}(d)-u_{j_{k'}}(d)|+L|d-x|
<\frac{2\epsilon}{3}.
\]
When \(L=0\), every \(u_j\) is constant on \(X_0\), and the same uniform Cauchy conclusion follows from convergence at the selected point.  Thus the subsequence is uniformly Cauchy.  Its pointwise limit on \(X_0\) is uniform, and the closedness just proved places that limit in \(\mathcal C_P\).  Every sequence therefore has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in the class; since the uniform norm is a metric, \(\mathcal C_P\) is compact.  Each defining inequality is preserved by convex combinations, so \(\mathcal C_P\) is convex.

For every finite Borel partition \((B_j)_{j=1}^m\) of \(X_0\), the definition of \(\nu_P\), the triangle inequality, and \(|S|=1\) almost surely give
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m|\nu_P(B_j)|
=\sum_{j=1}^m\left|E_P[S\mathbf 1\{X\in B_j\}]\right|
\le E_P\left[\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbf 1\{X\in B_j\}\right]
=1.
\]
Taking the supremum over finite partitions yields \(\|\nu_P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1\).  Therefore, by the definition of \(J_P\),
\[
|J_P(u)-J_P(v)|
\le \|\nu_P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\|u-v\|_\infty
\le \|u-v\|_\infty.
\]
Thus \(J_P\) is continuous.  On the assumed nonempty compact class it attains its minimum and maximum, which are precisely \(V_P^-\) and \(V_P^+\) by the frontier-value definition.  Since \(J_P\) is linear and \(\mathcal C_P\) is convex, \(J_P(\mathcal C_P)\) is convex; since it is also a nonempty compact subset of \(\mathbb R\),
\[
J_P(\mathcal C_P)=[V_P^-,V_P^+].
\]

In the setting of the full-law sharpness theorem, compact treatment support and the no-stayer condition imply
\[
0<A=E_P|Z|\le\operatorname{diam}(I)<\infty.
\]
The affine map \(v\mapsto(T-v)/A\) is continuous and reverses order.  The definition of \(\Theta(P)\), equivalently the already established full-law sharp characterization, therefore gives
\[
\Theta(P)
=\left[\frac{T-V_P^+}{A},\frac{T-V_P^-}{A}\right].
\]
It remains to prove the asserted deterministic bound.  For \(u\in\mathcal C_P\), \(S\) is measurable with respect to \((X,Z)\), and the definition of the conditional-mean version \(g\) gives
\[
E_P[S\Delta Y]=E_P[Sg(X,Z)].
\]
The definition of \(\nu_P\) gives \(J_P(u)=E_P[Su(X)]\).  Consequently the support-cone restriction in the definition of \(\mathcal C_P\) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
|T-J_P(u)|
&=|E_P[S\{g(X,Z)-u(X)\}]|\\
&\le E_P|g(X,Z)-u(X)|\\
&\le K E_P|Z|=KA.
\end{aligned}
\]
Division by \(A>0\) proves \((T-J_P(u))/A\in[-K,K]\) for every feasible \(u\), and hence \(\Theta(P)\subseteq[-K,K]\).

By the attained-interval theorem and \(A>0\), the nonempty set \(\Theta(P)\) is the closed interval
\[
\Theta(P)=
\left[\frac{T-V_P^+}{A},\frac{T-V_P^-}{A}\right].
\]
Its length is
\[
\frac{T-V_P^-}{A}-\frac{T-V_P^+}{A}
=\frac{V_P^+-V_P^-}{A}
=\frac{R(P)}{A},
\]
where the final equality is the definition of \(R(P)\).  A nonempty closed interval is a singleton if and only if its length is zero.  Because \(A>0\), this occurs if and only if \(V_P^+=V_P^-\), equivalently if and only if \(R(P)=0\).  Full-law sharpness identifies \(\Theta(P)\) with the set of causal values generated by legal completions, so this singleton condition is exactly point identification of WAOSS rather than merely uniqueness of an unrelated optimization functional.

For each positive integer \(k\), choose a regular conditional probability and write
\[
q_k(x)=P(|Z|\le 1/k\mid X=x).
\]
Since \(M_{1/k}=\mathbf 1\{|Z|>1/k\}\), the assumed inequality \(P(M_{1/k}=1\mid X)<1\) says that \(q_k(X)>0\) almost surely.  Fix \(x\in X_0\) and let \(U_k=(x-1/k,x+1/k)\).  By the definition of \(X_0=\operatorname{supp}_P(X)\),
\[
P(X\in U_k)>0.
\]
Because \(q_k>0\) for \(P_X\)-almost every baseline,
\[
P(X\in U_k,|Z|\le1/k)
=\int_{U_k}q_k(x')\,dP_X(x')>0.
\]
A positive-probability Borel set must meet the support \(H=\operatorname{supp}_P(X,Z)\).  Hence there is \((x_k,z_k)\in H\) with \(|x_k-x|<1/k\) and \(|z_k|\le1/k\).  Thus \((x_k,z_k)\to(x,0)\).  Since \(H\) is closed, it follows that
\[
(x,0)\in H\qquad\text{for every }x\in X_0.
\]
This argument uses only support neighborhoods and does not condition on a null singleton.

Under the compatibility clause in the proposition, at least one legal completion exists.  The full-law sharpness theorem then implies \(\mathcal C_P\ne\varnothing\).  For any \(u\in\mathcal C_P\), the support-cone inequality at \((x,0)\) gives
\[
|g(x,0)-u(x)|\le K|0|=0
\qquad(x\in X_0).
\]
Therefore every feasible function equals \(g(\cdot,0)\).  Nonemptiness shows that this function itself is feasible, so
\[
\mathcal C_P=\{x\mapsto g(x,0)\}.
\]
The frontier definitions consequently give
\[
V_P^-=V_P^+=\int_{X_0}g(x,0)\,d\nu_P(x),
\qquad
R(P)=0.
\]
Substitution into the attained sharp interval yields
\[
\Theta(P)=
\left\{\frac{T-\int_{X_0}g(x,0)\,d\nu_P(x)}{A}\right\}.
\]
This is the weighted WAOSS quasi-stayer-limit formula in Theorem 1 of de Chaisemartin, D'Haultf\oe{}uille, and Vazquez-Bare (2024).  The comparison with Assumption 5 and Theorem 3 of arXiv:2201.06898v1 is only an analogy in the support condition: that theorem concerns the distinct unweighted target \(\delta_1\), and no equality of estimands is used here.

Finally, the already established source-class recession-ray proposition supplies the declared continuous law \(P^{\circ}\).  At that law, baseline-conditional zero support fails on a set of \(P_X^{\circ}\)-probability \(p_{\circ}>0\), while the bounded sensitivity class has
\[
\Theta(P^{\circ})=
\left[-\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
       \frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}}\right].
\]
The interval is nondegenerate, so the point-identification proposition implies \(R(P^{\circ})>0\).  This proves the stated possibility claim; it does not assert that every failure of conditional support is sufficient for \(R(P)>0\).

Under \(P^{\diamond}\), the two atoms give
\[
(X,Z)=(-1/2,1/2)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(X,Z)=(1/2,-1/2),
\]
each with probability \(1/2\).  Therefore
\[
X_0=\{-1/2,1/2\},
\qquad
H=\{(-1/2,1/2),(1/2,-1/2)\}.
\]
Because \(Y_1=Y_2=0\) at both atoms, \(\Delta Y=0\), the support version of the conditional mean is \(g=0\), and \(T=0\).  Moreover,
\[
A=E_{P^{\diamond}}|Z|=\frac12,
\qquad
\nu_{P^{\diamond}}
=\frac12\delta_{-1/2}-\frac12\delta_{1/2}.
\]

With \(K=L=M=1\), direct substitution in the obstacle definitions gives, at either baseline, the local bounds \([-1/2,1/2]\).  The cone transported from the other baseline is weaker because the baselines are distance one apart.  Hence
\[
\ell_{P^{\diamond}}(-1/2)=\ell_{P^{\diamond}}(1/2)=-\frac12,
\qquad
r_{P^{\diamond}}(-1/2)=r_{P^{\diamond}}(1/2)=\frac12.
\]
Any two numbers in these intervals differ by at most one, so the one-Lipschitz constraint imposes no additional restriction.  The obstacle-compatibility theorem therefore gives
\[
\mathcal C_{P^{\diamond}}
=\{u:|u(-1/2)|\le1/2,\ |u(1/2)|\le1/2\}.
\]
For every such \(u\),
\[
J_{P^{\diamond}}(u)
=\frac{u(-1/2)-u(1/2)}2,
\qquad
\frac{T-J_{P^{\diamond}}(u)}A
=u(1/2)-u(-1/2).
\]
The last quantity has the attained range \([-1,1]\), so the attained-interval theorem gives \(\Theta(P^{\diamond})=[-1,1]\).

It remains to verify full-law attainment directly.  By definition,
\[
b_u^{\diamond}=
\begin{cases}
-2u(-1/2),&X=-1/2,\\
 2u(1/2),&X=1/2,
\end{cases}
\qquad
|b_u^{\diamond}|\le1.
\]
Evaluation of the schedules at the realized treatments gives
\[
Y_1^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(D_1)=0=Y_1,
\qquad
Y_2^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(D_2)=0=Y_2,
\]
so consistency holds and the entire observed law is unchanged.  For every \(d\in[-1,1]\), on the same event for all \(d\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_2^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(d)-Y_1^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(d)
&=b_u^{\diamond}(D_1-D_2)\\
&=-b_u^{\diamond}Z
=u(X).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both conditional expectations of the period difference, given \((X,Z)\) and given \(X\), equal \(u(X)\) simultaneously for every dose.  This verifies the strengthened common-event parallel-trends clause and gives \(m_{Q_u^{\diamond}}=u\).  Each schedule is individually one-Lipschitz because its slope is \(b_u^{\diamond}\).  The period-two causal movement is
\[
Y_2^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(D_2)-Y_2^{Q_u^{\diamond}}(D_1)
=b_u^{\diamond}Z=-u(X),
\]
whose conditional absolute mean is at most \(1/2=|Z|\).  Boundedness of the dose interval and the schedules gives latent integrability.  Hence every defining condition of the bounded-slope/Lipschitz sensitivity completion class holds, and
\[
\theta(Q_u^{\diamond})=u(1/2)-u(-1/2).
\]
If \(u(-1/2)=1/2\) and \(u(1/2)=-1/2\), then \(b_u^{\diamond}=-1\) at both atoms and \(\theta(Q_u^{\diamond})=-1\).  Reversing the signs gives \(b_u^{\diamond}=1\) and \(\theta(Q_u^{\diamond})=1\).  The construction uses two baseline values and opposite signs of \(Z\), so it is not the common-zero-baseline scalar design.

The two support rectangles in the definition of \(P^{\circ}\) each have Lebesgue area \(1/2\).  Their density integrals are therefore \(p_{\circ}\) and \(1-p_{\circ}\), which sum to one.  Since \(p_{\circ}\in(0,1)\), the density is bounded and strictly positive on each rectangle.  The outcomes are identically zero and hence bounded.  Absolute continuity gives \(P^{\circ}(Z=0)=0\), while the second rectangle gives
\[
P^{\circ}(|Z|\le\eta)>0
\qquad\text{for every }\eta>0.
\]
For every \(x\in[-1,0)\), however, the conditional support of \(Z\) is \([1/2,1]\), so baseline-conditional quasi-stayers fail there.  Integrating the first rectangle over \(z\) gives marginal density \(p_{\circ}\) for \(X\) on \([-1,0]\), and thus the failure region has probability \(p_{\circ}\).

The definitions yield
\[
X_0=[-1,1],
\qquad
H=[-1,0]\times[1/2,1]\ \cup\ [0,1]\times[-1/4,1/4],
\qquad
g=0,
\qquad
T=0.
\]
On the first rectangle \(S=1\).  On the second rectangle the conditional distribution of \(Z\) is uniform and symmetric about zero, so its conditional sign mean is zero.  Hence
\[
d\nu_{P^{\circ}}(x)
=p_{\circ}\mathbf 1\{x\in[-1,0]\}\,dx.
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
A
&=p_{\circ}E[Z\mid Z\in[1/2,1]]
 +(1-p_{\circ})E[|Z|\mid Z\in[-1/4,1/4]]\\
&=\frac{3p_{\circ}}4+\frac{1-p_{\circ}}8
=\frac{1+5p_{\circ}}8.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(x\in[0,1]\), \((x,0)\in H\), so the zero-change obstacle forces \(u(x)=0\).  For \(x\in[-1,0]\), the point \((x,1/2)\in H\) gives \(|u(x)|\le1/2\), while global one-Lipschitz continuity and \(u(0)=0\) give \(|u(x)|\le -x\).  Conversely, direct substitution in the obstacle-envelope definitions shows that no transported cone is tighter.  Thus
\[
r_{P^{\circ}}(x)=-\ell_{P^{\circ}}(x)
=\begin{cases}
\min\{-x,1/2\},&x\in[-1,0],\\
0,&x\in[0,1].
\end{cases}
\]
The upper and lower envelopes are themselves bounded, globally one-Lipschitz, and support-cone feasible.  By obstacle compatibility they attain the signed-objective extrema.  Therefore
\[
V_{P^{\circ}}^+
=p_{\circ}\int_{-1}^0\min\{-x,1/2\}\,dx
=\frac{3p_{\circ}}8,
\qquad
V_{P^{\circ}}^-=-\frac{3p_{\circ}}8.
\]
The attained-interval theorem now gives
\[
\Theta(P^{\circ})
=\left[-\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
         \frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}}\right].
\]

For \(s\in\{+,-\}\), evaluation of the displayed affine schedules at the realized doses gives
\[
Y_1^{Q_s^{\circ}}(D_1)=0=Y_1,
\qquad
Y_2^{Q_s^{\circ}}(D_2)=0=Y_2,
\]
so the entire observed law is preserved.  For every \(d\in[-2,2]\), on one event common to all doses,
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_2^{Q_s^{\circ}}(d)-Y_1^{Q_s^{\circ}}(d)
&=-\frac{u_s^{\circ}(X)}Z\{(d-D_2)-(d-X)\}\\
&=u_s^{\circ}(X).
\end{aligned}
\]
The two conditional expectations, given \((X,Z)\) and given \(X\), therefore both equal \(u_s^{\circ}(X)\) simultaneously for all \(d\).  Thus the strengthened parallel-trends clause holds and \(m_{Q_s^{\circ}}=u_s^{\circ}\).  Both trends are bounded by one and globally one-Lipschitz.  Moreover, \(|u_s^{\circ}(X)|\le|Z|\) on the first rectangle and \(u_s^{\circ}(X)=0\) on the second, so the common affine slope has magnitude at most one.  The period-two movement equals \(-u_s^{\circ}(X)\), proving the conditional mean-movement bound with \(K=1\).  Compact treatment support and bounded slopes imply latent integrability.  Hence \(Q_+^{\circ}\) and \(Q_-^{\circ}\) are legal sensitivity-class completions.  Finally, the causal definition gives
\[
\theta(Q_+^{\circ})
=-\frac{E_{P^{\circ}}[S u_+^{\circ}(X)]}{A}
=-\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
\qquad
\theta(Q_-^{\circ})
=\frac{3p_{\circ}}{1+5p_{\circ}},
\]
so the two displayed full laws attain the two endpoints.

Suppose \(P(X=0)=1\) and \(Z>0\) almost surely.  Then \(S=1\), \(X_0=\{0\}\), and, by the definition of the signed baseline measure,
\[
\nu_P=\delta_0.
\]
A continuous baseline trend is now a single scalar \(c=u(0)\); there is no nontrivial cross-baseline Lipschitz inequality.  The obstacle-envelope definitions reduce exactly to
\[
\underline c
=\max\left\{-M,\sup_{(0,z)\in H}\{g(0,z)-Kz\}\right\},
\qquad
\overline c
=\min\left\{M,\inf_{(0,z)\in H}\{g(0,z)+Kz\}\right\}.
\]
Indeed, \(c\in[\underline c,\overline c]\) is equivalent, term by term, to
\[
|c|\le M,
\qquad
|g(0,z)-c|\le Kz
\quad\text{for every }(0,z)\in H.
\]
Thus obstacle compatibility gives
\[
\mathcal C_P=\{c\in\mathbb R:\underline c\le c\le\overline c\},
\]
with the convention that this set is empty when \(\underline c>\overline c\).  Whenever the completion model is compatible, \(\underline c\le\overline c\).  Since \(J_P(c)=c\), the attained-interval formula then becomes
\[
\Theta(P)=
\left[\frac{T-\overline c}{A},
      \frac{T-\underline c}{A}\right].
\]
This is precisely the scalar intersection program obtained from the common-zero-baseline bounded conditional-average-slope inequalities.  It is the bounded-slope WAOSS interval reported by de Chaisemartin, Ciccia, D'Haultf\oe{}uille, and Knau (2024, arXiv:2405.04465v4, Section 4.2.1, Theorem 4, and Appendix B.2).  The present proposition proves only the algebraic reduction to that prior-art program and claims no novelty for the scalar case.

Fix a compatible \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}\).  On \(\mathcal E_n(P)\), the established uniform band-to-program theorem gives
\[
\widehat L_n
\le\frac{T-V_P^+}{A}
\le\frac{T-V_P^-}{A}
\le\widehat U_n.
\]
By the attained-interval theorem, the middle closed interval is exactly the sharp causal set \(\Theta(P)\).  Therefore
\[
\mathcal E_n(P)
\subseteq
\{\Theta(P)\subseteq[\widehat L_n,\widehat U_n]\}
=\{\Theta(P)\subseteq\widehat{\mathrm{CI}}_n\}.
\]
Taking probabilities, then the infimum over all \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}\) with \(\mathcal C_P\ne\varnothing\), and finally the lower limit, the uniform probability bound in the parent theorem yields
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}:\,\mathcal C_P\ne\varnothing}
P\{\Theta(P)\subseteq\widehat{\mathrm{CI}}_n\}
\ge1-\alpha.
\]
The attained-interval theorem also gives the deterministic inclusion \(\Theta(P)\subseteq[-K,K]\).  Consequently clipping the empirical endpoints to \([-K,K]\) cannot discard any true causal value.  Neither the event implication nor the uniform probability bound assumes \(R(P)>0\), strict obstacle inequalities, or a unique optimizer.  The conclusion therefore covers singleton frontiers, binding obstacles, and nonunique finite-program solutions.

proposed.condition:
There are jointly measurable versions of the two conditional expectations such that
\[
Q\!\left(\left\{\omega:
E_Q[Y_2^Q(d)-Y_1^Q(d)\mid X,Z](\omega)
=E_Q[Y_2^Q(d)-Y_1^Q(d)\mid X](\omega)
\text{ for every }d\in X_0\right\}\right)=1.
\]

novel.justification: de Chaisemartin, D'Haultf\oe{}uille, and Vazquez-Bare (2024) supply the per-dose conditional-parallel-trends condition. The single common full-probability event, together with joint measurability, is an additional strengthening needed to substitute the random diagonal dose \(d=X\). The bounded same-slope lift and the source recession-ray construction both satisfy the stronger equality simultaneously for every dose.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The source's per-dose almost-sure condition does not by itself permit substitution of the random diagonal dose \(d=X\). The replacement makes the required common full-probability event explicit. The established bounded same-slope lift and source recession-ray proofs both verify an identity common to every dose, so they satisfy this strengthened clause.

proposed.name: bounded-slope/Lipschitz sensitivity completion class \(\mathfrak Q(P)\)
proposed.construction:
The bounded-slope/Lipschitz sensitivity completion class is
\[
\mathfrak Q(P)=\left\{Q:\begin{array}{l}
Q\text{ is a law over the declared one-argument static schedules and matches the entire observed law }P;\\
\text{consistency and latent integrability hold; }g\in C(H);\\
\text{the simultaneous common-event conditional-parallel-trends condition holds on }X_0;\\
\left|E_Q[Y_2^Q(D_2)-Y_2^Q(D_1)\mid X,Z]\right|\le K|Z|\quad Q\text{-almost surely};\\
m_Q\in C(X_0),\quad \|m_Q\|_\infty\le M,\quad
|m_Q(x)-m_Q(x')|\le L|x-x'|\quad\text{for all }x,x'\in X_0
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
No marginal quasi-stayer restriction is part of this definition.  The finite \(K\) movement bound, the bounded globally \(L\)-Lipschitz trend, the continuous support version \(g\), and the simultaneous common-event clause are explicit sensitivity restrictions.  On an observed law satisfying the published assumptions, comparison with the source class concerns only source completions that also satisfy these restrictions.  No global equality or inclusion of completion classes is asserted, and the finite sharp interval for this sensitivity class does not transfer upward to the unrestricted published class.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The replacement names the positive model as a bounded-slope/Lipschitz sensitivity completion class, enumerates every extra restriction including the finite \(K\) movement bound, continuous support version, and simultaneous diagonal clause, records that marginal quasi-stayers are unnecessary, and prevents its finite sharp interval from being read as the unrestricted source-class identified set.

proposed.comparator_claim: Under Assumptions 1--4, including marginal quasi-stayers in Assumption 4, Theorem 1 states the weighted WAOSS quasi-stayer-limit formula; the regular witness shows that this singleton is not identified over that published class.
In arXiv:2201.06898v1, Section 4.1, Assumption 5 imposes baseline-conditional quasi-stayer support, and Theorem 3 identifies the unweighted switcher-slope target \(\delta_1\), not WAOSS.
Without quasi-stayers, bounded conditional average slopes yield sharp intersection bounds in the common-zero-baseline design.
The bounds obtained by solving finite linear programs are sharp under the paper's discrete-support shape restrictions.
The data can estimate an upper bound on the diameter of the identified set.
Identified IV-weighted averages restrict policy-relevant weighted averages of the same marginal treatment effects.
Calibrated projection controls coverage uniformly over a large class of moment-inequality models.
Least-squares series estimators admit uniform rates and confidence bands for conditional-mean functionals.
Boundary-adaptive local-polynomial estimators admit uniform Gaussian approximations and confidence bands.
Finite LP-value estimation is pointwise root-\(n\) consistent under feasibility and finiteness.
Bias correction for slow movers yields point-identified panel limit theory under weak treatment changes.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The published-class non-representability claim is now matched by the accepted source-class recession-ray proposition; the deleted marginal-gap identifier is stale.

prose_updates.tldr: Marginal quasi-stayers do not identify the weighted WAOSS singleton claimed by de Chaisemartin, D'Haultf\oe{}uille, and Vazquez-Bare (2024): at a regular heterogeneous-baseline witness, the published completion class contains an affine recession ray and its WAOSS image is all of \(\mathbb R\). The positive result is instead a sharp sensitivity-class characterization after the published singleton failure. Its completion class adds a finite \(K\) conditional mean-movement bound, bounded globally \(L\)-Lipschitz baseline trends, a continuous support version of \(g\), and a simultaneous common-event parallel-trends clause needed on the random diagonal. Marginal quasi-stayers are not required for this characterization, and its finite attained obstacle interval does not transfer to the unrestricted source class. Baseline-conditional zero support recovers the proceedings paper's weighted singleton formula; arXiv:2201.06898v1 Theorem 3 remains an analogous result for the distinct unweighted target \(\delta_1\). The finite outer program yields a uniformly honest interval on the fixed-support regular subclass, while fixed-support minimaxity as \(R(P)\to0\) remains open.

project_justification.gap: The proceedings paper states weighted WAOSS point identification under Assumptions 1--4, but marginal quasi-stayers do not imply the baseline-conditional positivity invoked immediately before display (4) of its Appendix proof. The regular witness gives a generic-class certificate of failure: the published completion class admits a legal affine recession ray whose WAOSS image is \(\mathbb R\). The source's per-dose parallel-trends clause also does not by itself license evaluation at the random diagonal dose; the sensitivity model therefore states its simultaneous common-event strengthening explicitly.
project_justification.niche: The paper separates three objects that cannot be conflated: the unrestricted published class, which is unbounded at the witness; a bounded-slope/Lipschitz sensitivity completion class with continuous \(g\) and a simultaneous diagonal clause, which has an exact finite obstacle interval; and the baseline-conditional zero-support regime, in which that interval collapses to the published weighted formula. On source-admissible observed laws, only the source completions also satisfying the added sensitivity restrictions are being characterized; no global class equality or inclusion is asserted.
project_justification.fill: The project proves the source-class recession-ray counterexample and then characterizes the strengthened sensitivity class by a full-observed-law affine lift, attained interval geometry, the exact criterion \(R(P)=0\), conditional-support singleton recovery, obstacle compatibility and constant-one clipping, certified finite programs, and uniform outer coverage on a fixed rectangle-support subclass. The common-zero-baseline scalar interval from arXiv:2405.04465v4 is retained solely as prior-art validation, and the source paper's separate parametric estimator is outside the challenge.

sampling_model.design: Independent and identically distributed two-period panel sampling from \(P\). Population analysis distinguishes the proceedings paper's Assumptions 1--4 completion class from the bounded-slope/Lipschitz sensitivity completion class used for the positive sharp characterization.
sampling_model.units: Each superpopulation unit has observed \(Y_1,Y_2,D_1,D_2\) and one-argument static potential-outcome schedules on the known compact interval \(I\). Conditional parallel trends in the sensitivity class is imposed through jointly measurable versions on one common full-probability event for every baseline dose, which makes evaluation at \(d=X\) legitimate. The source supplies only the per-dose condition; the common-event diagonal clause is an explicit strengthening.
